tool.name: Requests
tool.tagline: The simple, synchronous HTTP client most Python code uses
tool.description: Requests is the de facto standard HTTP library for Python: a small, readable API for sending GET, POST and other requests, handling JSON, headers, cookies, authentication and file uploads. It sits on top of urllib3, which provides connection pooling and retries. Learning it lets you call web APIs, download files and script any HTTP service from Python.

glossary.def: A popular add-on library for Python that sends HTTP requests with one simple function call, such as requests.get(url).
What Requests hands back after a request: one Python object holding the status code, headers and body of the server's answer.
In Requests, a Session object that remembers settings, cookies and open connections across many requests, so you set things up once and reuse them.
A Response method that raises an HTTPError exception when the status code is 400 or higher, and does nothing otherwise.
How long to wait while setting up the connection to the server before giving up.
How long to wait for the next piece of data from a server that is already connected; it resets each time data arrives.
The part of Requests that actually sends a prepared request over the network and builds the Response; you attach one to a session for URLs starting with a given prefix.
In Requests, to attach a transport adapter to a session for every URL that starts with a given prefix, like https://.
The lower-level Python library Requests is built on; it manages the actual network connections, pools and retries.
A request after Requests has filled in everything: the final URL, all headers and the body as bytes, exactly as it will be sent.
The body format browsers use to upload files: the body is split into parts (files and form fields), separated by a unique marker string.
A file listing the certificate authorities a program trusts when it checks a server's HTTPS certificate.
A secure connection where the client also shows a certificate, so the server can check who the client is, not just the other way round.
A function you give Requests to run automatically on every response, for example to log it.
A file in your home folder that stores user names and passwords per server; Requests reads it automatically when you pass no auth=.

concepts.name: Your first GET request
concepts.summary: Install Requests and fetch a URL with requests.get, then look at the status code and body.
concepts.why: Calling a web API or downloading a page takes one line with Requests, and every later lesson builds on it.
concepts.body:
Many services offer data to programs, not just to people: weather, exchange rates, your GitHub profile. A service that programs talk to over HTTP is a web API, often just called an **API**. **Requests** is the Python library most people use to talk to them. It isn't part of Python itself, so you install it once with Python's installer, `pip install requests`, and then `import requests`.

The module has one function per HTTP method: `requests.get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `head` and `options`. Each takes a URL plus optional keyword arguments, and, once the whole response has arrived, gives back a **Response object**: one Python object holding everything the server sent back.

```python
r = requests.get("https://api.github.com")
```

The response carries several values you read with a dot, like `r.status_code`. A value attached to an object this way is called an **attribute**. The most important ones:

- `r.status_code`: the HTTP status as an int, like `200` or `404`.
- `r.ok`: `True` when the status is below 400.
- `r.text`: the body as a `str`.
- `r.json()`: the body turned from JSON text into Python dicts and lists. Reading text and working out its structure like this is called **parsing**.
- `r.headers`: the response headers.

An error status is **not** an exception in Requests. `requests.get` happily returns a `404` response, and you must check it yourself (a later lesson shows `raise_for_status`). Exceptions are raised only when there is no response at all, for example when the domain name can't be found or the server refuses the connection.

Requests is **synchronous**: your program stops at the call and waits until the response is complete, then carries on. That is simple and fits scripts and most everyday programs. Programs that must keep thousands of requests going at the same time use other libraries, such as HTTPX, which work on the same ideas.

Always pass a `timeout` in real code, so a silent server can't make your program wait forever. It gets its own lesson later, but the examples use it from the start.
concepts.code:
import requests

r = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/get", timeout=10)

print(r.status_code)              # 200
print(r.ok)                       # True
print(r.headers["Content-Type"])  # application/json
data = r.json()
print(type(data).__name__)        # dict
print(data["url"])                # https://httpbin.org/get

missing = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/status/404", timeout=10)
print(missing.status_code, missing.ok)  # 404 False  (no exception!)
takeaways: requests.get/post/put/... return a Response
status_code, ok, text, json() and headers are the essentials
HTTP error statuses do not raise by default
pitfalls: Assuming requests.get raises an exception on 404 or 500.

quiz.q: What happens when requests.get(url) receives a 500 response?
options: It returns a Response with status_code 500
quiz.explain: Requests only raises when it gets no response at all; error statuses come back as normal Response objects.

concepts.name: The Response object
concepts.summary: Read a response's body as text, bytes or JSON, inspect headers and encoding, and see redirects and timing.
concepts.why: Getting data out of a response correctly, including encoding and JSON errors, is half of every HTTP task.
concepts.body:
A `Response` gives you the body in three forms:

- `r.content`: raw `bytes`. Use it for images, archives and any other binary data.
- `r.text`: the body turned into a `str` using the text encoding in `r.encoding`. Requests reads that from the `charset` part of the `Content-Type` header, which says how the server encoded its text.
- `r.json()`: parses the body as JSON. If the body is not valid JSON (an HTML error page, or an empty `204` response), it raises `requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError`.

When the header names no charset, Requests has to guess; for `text/*` types it falls back to ISO-8859-1, an old Western European encoding the early HTTP rules prescribed. If you know the server really sends UTF-8, set `r.encoding = "utf-8"` before reading `r.text`.

Headers live in `r.headers`, a dict that is **case-insensitive**: `r.headers["content-type"]` and `r.headers["Content-Type"]` are the same entry.

Other useful attributes:

- `r.url`: the final URL after redirects. `r.history` lists the redirect responses that led there. Requests follows redirects automatically for every method except `HEAD`; pass `allow_redirects=False` to stop that.
- `r.elapsed`: how long it took from sending the request until the response headers arrived, as a `timedelta` (Python's type for a length of time).
- `r.request`: the request that was actually sent, with its final URL, headers and body. When something goes wrong and you are hunting for the cause, which is called **debugging**, this shows exactly what left your program.
- `r.reason`: the status text, like `"Not Found"`.
- `r.cookies`: cookies the server set.

Check the status before trusting the body: calling `r.json()` on an error page is a common source of confusing exceptions.
concepts.code:
import requests

r = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/redirect/2", timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.url)          # 200 https://httpbin.org/get
print([h.status_code for h in r.history])  # [302, 302]
print(r.headers["content-type"])     # application/json  (case-insensitive)
print(type(r.content).__name__, type(r.text).__name__)  # bytes str
print(r.request.method, r.request.url)   # GET https://httpbin.org/get

html = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/html", timeout=10)
try:
    html.json()
except requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError:
    print("not JSON")                # not JSON

r2 = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/redirect/1", allow_redirects=False, timeout=10)
print(r2.status_code, r2.headers["Location"])  # 302 /get
takeaways: content is bytes, text is decoded str, json() parses JSON
headers is case-insensitive; url and history show redirects
r.request shows exactly what was sent
pitfalls: Reading r.text for binary data such as images; use r.content.

quiz.q: Which attribute should you use to save a downloaded PNG to disk?
quiz.explain: Images are binary, so you need the raw bytes in r.content.

concepts.name: Query parameters and headers
concepts.summary: Pass query strings with params= and custom headers with headers=, letting Requests handle encoding.
concepts.why: Almost every web API call needs query parameters, an Accept header or an API key, and building URLs by hand causes bugs.
concepts.body:
Never build query strings by gluing text together. Pass a dict to `params=` and Requests URL-encodes keys and values for you, including spaces, `&` and letters such as `é`:

```python
requests.get(url, params={"q": "rock & roll", "page": 2})
```

A value that is a list produces a repeated key (`tag=a&tag=b`). Keys whose value is `None` are left out, which is handy for optional filters. Parameters already in the URL are kept and the new ones added after them.

Custom headers go in `headers=` as a dict. Typical uses:

- `Accept: application/json` to ask for JSON.
- `User-Agent` to name your program; some APIs reject the default `python-requests/x.y`.
- `Authorization` to prove who you are. Many APIs give you an **API key**: a secret string, like a password for your program, that you send with each request.

A common form is `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, where the token is such a secret string. A later lesson covers the `auth=` argument, which does this more neatly.

Header values must be strings (or bytes); passing an int raises an error. Requests adds a few headers of its own (`User-Agent`, `Accept-Encoding`, `Accept`, `Connection`), and yours replace them. Setting a header to `None` removes one of those defaults.

Leave `Content-Type` and `Content-Length` to Requests when you use `json=`, `data=` or `files=`; it sets them for you. For file uploads in particular, Requests has to put a special separator string into `Content-Type`, and a header you set by hand won't have it, so the upload breaks.

Look at `r.url` or `r.request.headers` to see exactly what was sent.
concepts.code:
import requests

r = requests.get(
    "https://httpbin.org/get",
    params={"q": "rock & roll", "tag": ["a", "b"], "page": 2, "skip": None},
    headers={"Accept": "application/json", "User-Agent": "my-script/1.0"},
    timeout=10,
)
print(r.url)
# https://httpbin.org/get?q=rock+%26+roll&tag=a&tag=b&page=2
echo = r.json()
print(echo["args"])              # {'page': '2', 'q': 'rock & roll', 'tag': ['a', 'b']}
print(echo["headers"]["User-Agent"])    # my-script/1.0
print(r.request.headers["Accept-Encoding"])  # gzip, deflate (default; may add br, zstd)
takeaways: params= builds and encodes the query string; None values are dropped
headers= adds or replaces headers; values must be strings
Let Requests set Content-Type for json=, data= and files=
pitfalls: Formatting URLs with f-strings like f'{url}?q={term}', which breaks on spaces and &.

quiz.q: What URL does requests.get('https://x.org/s', params={'q': 'a b', 'n': None}) request?
quiz.explain: Values are URL-encoded (space becomes +) and keys with None are omitted.

concepts.name: Sending JSON, forms and other bodies
concepts.summary: Send request bodies with json=, data= and files= using POST, PUT and PATCH, and know which Content-Type each sets.
concepts.why: Creating or changing data through a web API means sending a body in the format the server expects.
concepts.body:
GET only asks for something. To create or change data on a server you send a request with a **body**, and Requests offers three ways to fill it. Each also sets the matching `Content-Type` header for you:

- `json=obj` turns a dict or list into JSON text and sets `Content-Type: application/json`. This is what most modern web APIs expect.
- `data=dict` sends the dict's keys and values the way a browser submits a simple HTML form (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`).
- `files={"field": file_obj}` uploads files as `multipart/form-data`, the format browsers use for file uploads (covered in a later lesson).

There is a fourth, rawer form. `data="some text"` (a string or bytes) sends exactly what you give it and adds no `Content-Type`. Use it for other text formats, such as XML (an older format of tags like `<name>Ada</name>`), and set the header yourself.

The methods are the usual HTTP ones: `post` to create, `put` to replace, `patch` to change part of something, `delete` to remove. They all accept the same keyword arguments as `get`.

Two classic mistakes:

- Using `data=` when the API wants JSON. `data={"a": 1}` sends `a=1` as a form, and a JSON API will answer `400` or `415`. Use `json=`.
- Passing both `json=` and `data=`: when `data` is given, `json` is ignored.

The response to a create call is often `201 Created`, with the new item in the body and its URL in the `Location` header. Some APIs answer `204 No Content`; there is no body, so `r.json()` would fail.
concepts.code:
import requests

base = "https://httpbin.org"

r = requests.post(f"{base}/post", json={"name": "Ada", "tags": ["math"]}, timeout=10)
echo = r.json()
print(echo["headers"]["Content-Type"])   # application/json
print(echo["json"])                      # {'name': 'Ada', 'tags': ['math']}

r = requests.post(f"{base}/post", data={"name": "Ada", "lang": "en"}, timeout=10)
echo = r.json()
print(echo["headers"]["Content-Type"])   # application/x-www-form-urlencoded
print(echo["form"])                      # {'lang': 'en', 'name': 'Ada'}

xml = "<user><name>Ada</name></user>"
r = requests.put(f"{base}/put", data=xml,
                 headers={"Content-Type": "application/xml"}, timeout=10)
print(r.json()["data"])                  # <user><name>Ada</name></user>
print(requests.delete(f"{base}/delete", timeout=10).status_code)  # 200
takeaways: json= for JSON APIs, data= for forms or raw bodies, files= for uploads
Each sets Content-Type, except raw data= strings and bytes
post, put, patch and delete take the same arguments as get
pitfalls: Sending data={'a': 1} to a JSON API and getting a 400 or 415 back.

quiz.q: You call requests.post(url, data={'a': 1}). What Content-Type does the request have?
quiz.explain: A dict passed as data is form-encoded; use json= for JSON.

concepts.name: Errors and raise_for_status
concepts.summary: Turn HTTP error statuses into exceptions with raise_for_status and handle the Requests exception hierarchy.
concepts.why: Robust code must distinguish network failures, timeouts and server errors, and react to each correctly.
concepts.body:
Since error statuses do not raise on their own, the usual habit is to call `r.raise_for_status()` right after the request. It does nothing for statuses below 400 and raises `requests.HTTPError` for 4xx and 5xx. The exception carries the response as `err.response`, so you can still read the status and the error body.

All Requests exceptions inherit from `requests.RequestException` (itself a subclass of Python's `OSError`). The important subclasses:

- `ConnectionError`: the domain name couldn't be found, the server refused the connection, or the network is down. Note this is `requests.ConnectionError`, not Python's built-in `ConnectionError`.
- `Timeout`: with subclasses `ConnectTimeout` and `ReadTimeout`.
- `HTTPError`: raised by `raise_for_status`.
- `TooManyRedirects`, `InvalidURL`, `MissingSchema` (you forgot `https://`), and `SSLError` (the secure HTTPS connection couldn't be set up; a subclass of `ConnectionError`).
- `JSONDecodeError` from `r.json()`.

Catch the most specific exception you can actually handle, and let the rest pass up to whoever called your function. A common structure:

- catch `Timeout` and `ConnectionError` to try again or report "service unreachable",
- catch `HTTPError` and branch on `err.response.status_code` (404 means not found, 401 means log in again, 5xx might be worth retrying),
- catch `RequestException` last as a fallback.

Avoid a bare `except Exception` around requests: it also hides mistakes in your own code, like a typo in a variable name. And remember that `raise_for_status` only works if you call it; forgetting it is the usual reason an error page ends up in `r.json()`.
takeaways: Call raise_for_status() after requests to turn 4xx/5xx into HTTPError
err.response gives access to the failed response
Catch specific exceptions; RequestException is the base class
pitfalls: Catching Python's built-in ConnectionError instead of requests.ConnectionError.

quiz.q: Which exception does raise_for_status() raise for a 503 response?

concepts.name: Timeouts
concepts.summary: Always set timeout=, understand connect versus read timeouts, and know what a timeout does not limit.
concepts.why: Without a timeout, one stuck server can hang your program forever.
concepts.body:
By default Requests has **no timeout**: if the server accepts the connection and then never answers, `requests.get` waits forever. Any code that runs for real should pass `timeout=` on every call. Code-checking tools such as Ruff and Bandit warn about calls without it.

`timeout` can be a single number or a `(connect, read)` tuple, in seconds:

- The **connect timeout** limits how long setting up the connection to the server may take (for HTTPS, that includes agreeing on encryption). Values just above a multiple of 3, such as 3.05, are often recommended, because computers resend an unanswered connection attempt after 3 seconds.
- The **read timeout** limits how long to wait **between pieces of data** from the server once connected. It is not a limit on the total download time: a server trickling one byte every few seconds can keep a request alive far longer than the read timeout.

When they fire you get `requests.ConnectTimeout` or `requests.ReadTimeout`, both subclasses of `requests.Timeout`. A connect timeout is safe to retry, since the request never reached the server. A read timeout is ambiguous for methods that aren't idempotent, like `POST`: the server may already have done the work.

If you need a hard deadline for the whole operation, you have to enforce it yourself: read the body in pieces and check the clock (see the streaming lesson), or run the call in the background and stop waiting after the deadline. HTTPX offers finer timeout settings if this matters a lot.

Note that `timeout=None` explicitly means wait forever.
concepts.code:
import time
import requests

try:
    requests.get("https://httpbin.org/delay/3", timeout=1)
except requests.ReadTimeout as e:
    print("read timeout")          # read timeout

t = time.perf_counter()
r = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/delay/1", timeout=(3.05, 5))
print(r.status_code, round(time.perf_counter() - t))  # 200 1

for exc in (requests.ConnectTimeout, requests.ReadTimeout):
    print(exc.__name__, issubclass(exc, requests.Timeout))
# ConnectTimeout True
# ReadTimeout True
takeaways: Requests waits forever unless you pass timeout=
timeout=(connect, read); read limits the gap between bytes, not total time
Connect timeouts are safe to retry; read timeouts may mean the server acted
pitfalls: Believing timeout=10 caps a large download at 10 seconds.

quiz.q: A server sends one byte every 4 seconds for a minute. With timeout=5, what happens?
options: The request completes after about a minute
quiz.explain: The read timeout resets with each received byte, so a slow but steady response never triggers it.

concepts.name: Sessions: connection reuse and defaults
concepts.summary: Use requests.Session to reuse connections, keep cookies and share headers, auth and other defaults across calls.
concepts.why: Sessions make repeated calls to one API faster and keep you logged in, and they are how real clients are structured.
concepts.body:
Every top-level `requests.get` opens a fresh connection and throws it away afterwards. A `requests.Session` is an object that remembers things between requests. Three things, mainly.

**Open connections.** Setting up a connection costs time: a TCP handshake and, for HTTPS, a TLS handshake too. A session keeps finished connections open and reuses them for the next request to the same host (the same server name and port). This store of ready connections is a **connection pool**. For many calls to one API it is often a large speedup.

**Cookies.** Cookies set by responses are stored in `s.cookies` and sent automatically on later requests, so logins work like in a browser.

**Defaults.** Attributes like `s.headers`, `s.params`, `s.auth`, `s.verify` and `s.proxies` apply to every request. Per-request arguments are merged with them: for dicts, a per-request key wins over the session's, and setting a key to `None` removes it for that one request.

Use a session in a `with` block so its connections are closed when you are done:

```python
with requests.Session() as s:
    s.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
    s.get(...)
```

In a larger program, create one session per API you talk to (for example inside a small wrapper class that also stores the API's base URL) and reuse it, instead of making a session for each request.

One gotcha: there is no session-wide `timeout` setting. Setting `s.timeout = 5` does nothing. Pass `timeout=` on each call, or wrap the session (a subclass that overrides `request`, or a helper function) to apply a default.
concepts.code:
import requests

with requests.Session() as s:
    s.headers.update({"User-Agent": "demo/1.0", "Accept": "application/json"})
    s.params = {"api_key": "abc"}

    s.get("https://httpbin.org/cookies/set/session_id/42", timeout=10)
    print(s.cookies.get("session_id"))          # 42

    r = s.get("https://httpbin.org/get", params={"page": 1}, timeout=10)
    echo = r.json()
    print(echo["args"])        # {'api_key': 'abc', 'page': '1'}  (merged)
    print(echo["headers"]["User-Agent"])        # demo/1.0

    r = s.get("https://httpbin.org/headers", headers={"Accept": None}, timeout=10)
    print("Accept" in r.json()["headers"])      # False: removed for this request

    r = s.get("https://httpbin.org/cookies", timeout=10)
    print(r.json())                              # {'cookies': {'session_id': '42'}}
takeaways: A Session reuses connections and keeps cookies
Session headers, params, auth and verify are merged into each request
There is no session-level timeout; pass timeout= per request
pitfalls: Creating a new Session for every request, which throws away connection reuse.

quiz.q: You set s.timeout = 5 on a Session. What timeout do requests made with s.get(url) use?
quiz.explain: Session has no timeout setting; the attribute is ignored and requests wait indefinitely unless timeout= is passed.

concepts.name: Authentication
concepts.summary: Authenticate with Basic auth, bearer tokens and custom AuthBase classes, and keep credentials out of code.
concepts.why: Nearly every real API requires credentials, and handling them correctly keeps your secrets safe.
concepts.body:
The `auth=` argument attaches credentials to a request. Common schemes:

- **Basic auth**: `auth=("user", "pass")`, a shortcut for `HTTPBasicAuth`. The password is only base64-encoded, not encrypted, so use it over HTTPS only.
- **Digest auth**: `HTTPDigestAuth("user", "pass")`, rare today.
- **Bearer tokens** (access tokens, API keys): set the header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, per request or on a session's `headers`.
- **API keys** in a custom header such as `X-API-Key`, or occasionally in the query string.

For anything custom, subclass `requests.auth.AuthBase` and write a `__call__(self, r)` method. Requests calls it with the prepared request (the request with its final URL, headers and body), and you return it after adding headers. This keeps auth logic in one place and lets you set `session.auth = MyAuth(...)`. Schemes where the client signs each request, computing a secret-keyed fingerprint of the body, are written this way.

Requests also reads credentials from a `.netrc` file in your home folder when you pass no `auth=`. That surprises people when a header they set by hand gets replaced, so be aware of it.

Security habits:

- Don't write secrets into your code files. Read them from **environment variables**: named settings the operating system hands to your program when it starts, like `API_TOKEN=...`.
- In bigger setups, a **secrets manager** (a service that stores passwords and keys and hands them only to programs allowed to have them) does this job.
- Requests drops the `Authorization` header when a redirect leads to a different server, so your credentials don't leak to someone else.
- Never log full request headers.

For OAuth 2 (the sign-in flow behind "Log in with Google" that fetches and renews tokens), use a library such as `requests-oauthlib` or `authlib` rather than writing it by hand.
concepts.code:
import os
import requests
from requests.auth import AuthBase

r = requests.get("https://httpbin.org/basic-auth/ada/s3cret",
                 auth=("ada", "s3cret"), timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.json())   # 200 {'authenticated': True, 'user': 'ada'}

class BearerAuth(AuthBase):
    def __init__(self, token):
        self.token = token
    def __call__(self, r):       # r is the PreparedRequest
        r.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self.token}"
        return r

token = os.environ.get("API_TOKEN", "demo-token")
with requests.Session() as s:
    s.auth = BearerAuth(token)
    r = s.get("https://httpbin.org/bearer", timeout=10)
    print(r.json())              # {'authenticated': True, 'token': 'demo-token'}

print(requests.get("https://httpbin.org/bearer", timeout=10).status_code)  # 401
takeaways: auth=(user, pass) for Basic; an Authorization header or AuthBase for tokens
AuthBase.__call__ changes the prepared request; set it on a session
Load secrets from the environment; Authorization is dropped on redirects to another server
pitfalls: Writing API tokens directly in code that later gets shared or published.

quiz.q: What must the __call__ method of a custom AuthBase return?
quiz.explain: Requests passes the PreparedRequest through the auth object and uses whatever it returns.

concepts.name: Testing code that uses Requests
concepts.summary: Test code that makes HTTP calls without a network, by faking responses with the responses library or a fake session.
concepts.why: Tests that call real APIs are slow, fail at random when the network hiccups, and can't easily fake errors; fake responses make them fast and repeatable.
concepts.body:
Code that calls an API should be tested without the API. Two common approaches.

The **responses** library (`pip install responses`) plugs into Requests at the point where a request would go out over the network, and answers registered URLs with replies you prepared. Inside `@responses.activate` (or the `responses.RequestsMock()` context manager), any request to a URL you didn't register raises `ConnectionError`, so tests can never touch the network by accident.

You can register JSON bodies, status codes, headers, exceptions to raise (`body=requests.ConnectionError()`), or a function that builds the reply. Afterwards, check `responses.calls` to see exactly what your code sent.

The other approach is to let the code be handed what it needs instead of creating it itself, which is called **dependency injection**. Write functions and clients to accept a `Session` (or a client object) as a parameter. Tests then pass a fake, such as `unittest.mock.Mock(spec=requests.Session)`. This works with any testing tool, and in the real program it makes sharing one session easy.

What to test:

- the normal case parses the data correctly,
- error statuses (404, 500) and network errors lead to the behaviour you want,
- the request is right: URL, query parameters, headers, JSON body,
- a timeout is passed (check the call's arguments).

Tests against a real service are worth having too, but keep them separate and opt-in (for example behind a pytest marker). Point them at a local test server, or replay saved recordings of real responses (`vcrpy`, `pytest-recording`), rather than the live service.
takeaways: The responses library intercepts Requests and blocks unregistered URLs
Accepting a session parameter makes code easy to fake
Test error cases and the exact request sent, not just success
pitfalls: Writing unit tests that call real third-party APIs.

quiz.q: Inside @responses.activate, what happens when code requests a URL that was not registered?
options: The real network request is made
quiz.explain: responses blocks unregistered URLs with ConnectionError so tests stay offline.

concepts.name: Retries with HTTPAdapter and urllib3
concepts.summary: Configure automatic retries with backoff by mounting an HTTPAdapter with a urllib3 Retry policy on a session.
concepts.why: Brief failures (dropped connections, 502, 503, 429) are normal when you make many calls; a retry policy quietly absorbs them.
concepts.body:
Requests does not retry failed requests by default. To add a policy, you configure the layer underneath it. Requests is built on **urllib3**, a lower-level library that manages the actual connections. The piece of Requests that hands a request to urllib3 is a **transport adapter** (`HTTPAdapter`), and you attach, or **mount**, one on a session for every URL that starts with a prefix:

```python
retry = Retry(total=5, backoff_factor=0.5, status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504])
s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))
```

Important `Retry` options:

- `total`, `connect`, `read`, `status`: the overall limit and limits per kind of failure.
- `backoff_factor`: exponential backoff. The first retry happens at once, then urllib3 sleeps `backoff_factor * 2 ** (n - 1)` seconds, where n counts the failures so far. So 0.1 gives 0, 0.2, 0.4 and so on, capped by `backoff_max`. Add `backoff_jitter` (random jitter) so many clients don't all retry at the same instant.
- `status_forcelist`: response statuses that should be retried.
- `allowed_methods`: by default only **idempotent** methods (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE) are retried. `POST` is left out because repeating it could create duplicates. Add it only if the API supports idempotency keys.
- `respect_retry_after_header` (default `True`): waits as long as a `Retry-After` header on a 429 or 503 asks.
- `raise_on_status`: when retries run out on a status, raise `requests.exceptions.RetryError` (the default) or return the last response.

Retries multiply the worst-case wait: each attempt can take up to the timeout, plus the backoff. Plan the total time accordingly, and log retries so a service that keeps failing doesn't go unnoticed.
concepts.code:
import time
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util import Retry

retry = Retry(
    total=3,
    backoff_factor=0.1,
    status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
    allowed_methods={"GET", "PUT", "DELETE"},
)
with requests.Session() as s:
    s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))
    s.mount("http://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

    t = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        s.get("https://httpbin.org/status/503", timeout=5)
    except requests.exceptions.RetryError as e:
        print("gave up:", type(e).__name__)      # gave up: RetryError
    print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s with backoff")  # about 0.6s

    r = s.post("https://httpbin.org/status/503", timeout=5)
    print(r.status_code)                         # 503  (POST is not retried)
takeaways: Mount HTTPAdapter(max_retries=Retry(...)) on a session to retry
status_forcelist and backoff_factor define what and how fast to retry
Only idempotent methods are retried by default; POST needs care
pitfalls: Retrying POST requests blindly and creating duplicate orders or payments.

quiz.q: Why does urllib3's Retry exclude POST from allowed_methods by default?
options: Retrying a non-idempotent request may perform the action twice
quiz.explain: If the first POST reached the server, a retry could duplicate its effect.

concepts.name: Streaming downloads and file uploads
concepts.summary: Download large files in pieces with stream=True instead of all at once, and upload files as multipart or streamed bodies.
concepts.why: Large files break the default load-everything behaviour, and uploads have their own body formats.
concepts.body:
By default Requests downloads the entire body into memory before returning. For large files, pass `stream=True`: only the headers are read, and you then take the body piece by piece as it arrives. This is called **streaming**. Use `r.iter_content(chunk_size=...)` for bytes, or `r.iter_lines()` for formats sent one line at a time, such as JSON Lines (one JSON value per line).

While you stream, the connection stays busy until the body is fully read or the response is closed. Use the response in a `with` block, `with s.get(url, stream=True) as r:`, so the connection goes back to the session's pool even if you stop early. `iter_content` undoes gzip compression for you; `r.raw` gives the untouched, still-compressed bytes if you really need them.

For **uploads**, there are two shapes:

- **Multipart form uploads**, as browsers do: `files={"file": open("report.pdf", "rb")}`, or a tuple `("name.pdf", fileobj, "application/pdf")` to set the file name and content type. You can combine `files=` with `data=` for extra form fields. Open files in binary mode.
- **Streaming the body**: pass a file object or a generator as `data=`. A file is sent straight from disk without reading it all into memory first. A generator's body is sent in pieces without announcing its total size up front, which HTTP calls chunked transfer encoding.

Note that `files=` builds the whole multipart body in memory. For very large multipart uploads, the `requests-toolbelt` package has a streaming `MultipartEncoder`.
concepts.code:
import requests

with requests.Session() as s:
    with s.get("https://httpbin.org/bytes/100000", stream=True, timeout=10) as r:
        r.raise_for_status()
        size = 0
        with open("download.bin", "wb") as f:
            for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=16_384):
                f.write(chunk)
                size += len(chunk)
    print(size)                                   # 100000

    with open("download.bin", "rb") as f:
        r = s.post("https://httpbin.org/post",
                   files={"upload": ("data.bin", f, "application/octet-stream")},
                   data={"note": "test"}, timeout=10)
    echo = r.json()
    print(echo["form"], list(echo["files"]))      # {'note': 'test'} ['upload']
    print(echo["headers"]["Content-Type"][:30])   # multipart/form-data; boundary=
takeaways: stream=True plus iter_content downloads in chunks
Use the streamed response as a context manager to release the connection
files= sends multipart; a file object or generator as data= streams the body
pitfalls: Opening upload files in text mode instead of 'rb'.

quiz.q: You call requests.get(url, stream=True) and only read the headers. What should you do?
options: Nothing, the body is discarded automatically
Close the response (or use it in a with block) to release the connection
Call r.json() to finish the request
quiz.explain: With streaming the connection stays checked out until the body is consumed or the response is closed.

concepts.name: TLS verification, certificates and proxies
concepts.summary: Control certificate checks with verify=, use client certificates, and send traffic through proxies, including settings from the environment.
concepts.why: Company networks, internal certificate authorities and client certificates are everyday realities, and turning checks off is the wrong fix.
concepts.body:
Requests checks every HTTPS certificate by default. It trusts the certificate authorities listed in a **CA bundle** file shipped with the `certifi` package. A failed check raises `requests.exceptions.SSLError`.

Some companies run their own internal certificate authority, which isn't in that bundle. Don't turn checking off. Point Requests at a bundle that includes it:

- `verify="/path/to/ca-bundle.pem"` per request or on a session,
- or the `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` environment variable (a setting passed to your program from outside; `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` works too).

`verify=False` disables all checks. Then anyone between you and the server can pretend to be the server and read or change your traffic. Requests prints an `InsecureRequestWarning` for each such request. Keep it for throwaway local experiments.

With **mutual TLS**, the server also checks who the client is, by the client's own certificate. Pass `cert=("client.crt", "client.key")`, or a single `.pem` file containing both.

A **proxy** is a middle server that forwards your traffic; company networks often require one. Configure it with `proxies={"http": "...", "https": "..."}`, keyed by the scheme of the target URL. Proxy URLs can contain credentials (`http://user:pass@proxy:3128`). SOCKS proxies, a more general kind, work after `pip install requests[socks]` with a `socks5h://` URL (the `h` makes the proxy look up domain names too).

Requests also reads settings from the environment: `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` and `.netrc` credentials. `session.trust_env` (default `True`) controls this. Setting it to `False` makes behaviour independent of the environment, which can help in tests but surprises users who rely on company proxy settings. Environment settings beat session attributes like `s.verify` in some cases, while per-request arguments always win.
concepts.code:
import requests

s = requests.Session()
print(s.verify, s.trust_env)            # True True

# Internal CA: point at the bundle, don't disable verification
# s.verify = "/etc/ssl/certs/corp-ca.pem"

# Mutual TLS: client certificate and key
# s.cert = ("client.crt", "client.key")

s.proxies = {"https": "http://proxy.internal:3128"}
print(s.proxies["https"])               # http://proxy.internal:3128

settings = s.merge_environment_settings(
    "https://example.com", proxies={}, stream=None, verify=None, cert=None)
print(sorted(settings))                 # ['cert', 'proxies', 'stream', 'verify']

try:
    requests.get("https://self-signed.badssl.com/", timeout=10)
except requests.exceptions.SSLError:
    print("certificate rejected")        # certificate rejected
except requests.ConnectionError:
    print("no network")
takeaways: Checks are on by default; fix certificate errors with verify=path or REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE
cert= supplies a client certificate for mutual TLS
proxies= and the HTTP(S)_PROXY / NO_PROXY variables route traffic; trust_env controls env use
pitfalls: Setting verify=False to silence an SSLError in code that runs for real.

quiz.q: Your company runs its own internal certificate authority and requests raises SSLError. What is the right fix?
quiz.explain: Trusting the company's certificate authority keeps checking on while accepting the internal certificates.

concepts.name: Prepared requests and the request lifecycle
concepts.summary: Follow a request from Request to PreparedRequest to adapter, and use prepared requests to inspect or tweak exactly what is sent.
concepts.why: Debugging odd API behaviour and building advanced clients requires knowing how your arguments become the bytes that are actually sent.
concepts.body:
`requests.get(...)` is a thin wrapper. Inside, a request goes through four steps:

- A `Request` object is created from your arguments: method, URL, headers, params, data, json, files, auth, cookies, hooks.
- `Session.prepare_request` merges it with the session's defaults (headers, cookies, auth, params) and calls `PreparedRequest.prepare`. That builds the final URL with the encoded query string, the body bytes, the `Content-Type` and `Content-Length` headers, and applies auth (including `.netrc`).
- `Session.send` merges settings from the environment (proxies, `verify`, `cert`, when `trust_env` is true), picks the **transport adapter** whose mounted prefix best matches the URL, and calls `adapter.send`.
- The adapter turns the prepared request into a urllib3 call and builds a `Response`. `Session.send` then runs **response hooks**, stores cookies, and follows redirects by building new prepared requests (`resolve_redirects`). That step also changes the method to GET after a 303 and strips credentials when the server changes.

You can run these steps yourself: `req = requests.Request("POST", url, json=...)`, `prep = s.prepare_request(req)`, adjust `prep.headers` or `prep.body`, then `s.send(prep, timeout=...)`. This is useful for signing the exact bytes being sent, for logging them, and for sending something the high-level functions would tidy up.

Note that `send` does not call `merge_environment_settings` for you; call it yourself if you need proxy and certificate settings from the environment. Also, after preparation `prep.body` is bytes or a string, not your dict.
concepts.code:
import hashlib
import requests

with requests.Session() as s:
    s.headers["User-Agent"] = "lifecycle-demo"
    req = requests.Request("POST", "https://httpbin.org/post",
                           params={"v": 2}, json={"id": 7})
    prep = s.prepare_request(req)          # merges session defaults

    print(prep.url)                        # https://httpbin.org/post?v=2
    print(prep.body)                       # b'{"id": 7}'
    print(prep.headers["Content-Type"])    # application/json
    print(prep.headers["User-Agent"])      # lifecycle-demo

    prep.headers["X-Body-SHA256"] = hashlib.sha256(prep.body).hexdigest()[:12]
    settings = s.merge_environment_settings(prep.url, {}, None, None, None)
    r = s.send(prep, timeout=10, **settings)
    print(r.json()["headers"]["X-Body-Sha256"])  # ad559f4e2220
takeaways: Request -> prepare_request (merge defaults) -> PreparedRequest -> adapter.send
Prepared requests expose the final URL, headers and body bytes
Session.send skips environment merging; call merge_environment_settings yourself
pitfalls: Expecting s.send(prep) to pick up proxy and CA settings from the environment automatically.

quiz.q: Which object holds the final encoded body bytes that go on the wire?
quiz.explain: Preparation turns the Request's high-level arguments into the final URL, headers and body.

concepts.name: Connection pooling and thread safety
concepts.summary: Tune urllib3 connection pools through HTTPAdapter and use Requests safely from several threads.
concepts.why: Clients making many requests at once hit pool limits and threading problems that never show up at low volume.
concepts.body:
Each `HTTPAdapter` owns a urllib3 `PoolManager`, which keeps one **connection pool per host** (scheme, host and port). Three parameters control it:

- `pool_connections`: how many per-host pools to keep (default 10). Talking to more hosts than this throws pools away, and with them the open connections.
- `pool_maxsize`: how many connections each pool keeps for reuse (default 10). If more threads than this send to one host at the same time, extra connections are opened and then **discarded** after use, with the warning "Connection pool is full, discarding connection". The number of requests you get through per second drops, because new TLS handshakes happen all the time.
- `pool_block=True` makes threads wait for a free connection instead of opening extra ones, capping how many requests run at once per host.

So for a thread pool (a fixed group of threads taking jobs from a queue) of 32 workers calling one API, mount `HTTPAdapter(pool_maxsize=32)`.

**Thread safety**: Requests does not formally promise that `Session` is thread-safe. In practice the connection pool is, and sharing one session for simple GETs is widely done. But the session's changeable state is not protected: cookies updated by responses arriving at once, or code changing `s.headers` while other threads send, can mix up badly. Safer patterns are one session per thread (`threading.local`), or a shared session whose settings never change after setup and that doesn't depend on cookies.

A connection returns to the pool only when the response body has been fully read or the response closed. Forgetting to close streamed responses is the classic cause of an empty pool.

For thousands of requests at once, threads plus Requests get expensive; an async client such as HTTPX or aiohttp, built on Python's `async`/`await`, is the better tool.
concepts.code:
import threading
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter

local = threading.local()

def get_session():
    if not hasattr(local, "s"):                   # one session per thread
        s = requests.Session()
        s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(pool_connections=4, pool_maxsize=8))
        s.mount("http://", HTTPAdapter(pool_connections=4, pool_maxsize=8))
        local.s = s
    return local.s

def fetch(i):
    r = get_session().get("https://httpbin.org/get", params={"i": i}, timeout=10)
    return r.json()["args"]["i"]

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(fetch, range(20)))
print(results[:5], len(results))                  # ['0', '1', '2', '3', '4'] 20
takeaways: An HTTPAdapter's pool keeps pool_maxsize connections per host
Size pool_maxsize to your thread count or connections are discarded
Prefer one session per thread or treat a shared session as read-only
pitfalls: Seeing 'Connection pool is full, discarding connection' and ignoring it.

quiz.q: 32 threads share a session with the default adapter and call one host. What happens?
options: Extra connections are created and discarded after use, so they aren't reused
Requests are queued over one connection
quiz.explain: Without pool_block the pool opens extra connections but only keeps pool_maxsize=10 of them for reuse.

concepts.name: Event hooks and custom transport adapters
concepts.summary: Run code on every response with hooks, and replace the transport itself by writing and mounting a custom adapter.
concepts.why: Hooks and adapters are how logging, measurements, caching and transports that don't use the network plug into Requests cleanly.
concepts.body:
Requests has two extension points besides auth.

**Event hooks.** The only hook is `"response"`: a function that receives the `Response` (plus keyword arguments such as `timeout` and `verify`) after it arrives. Register it per request (`hooks={"response": fn}`) or on a session (`s.hooks["response"].append(fn)`). If the hook returns a value, that value replaces the response; returning `None` keeps it. Typical uses are logging, counting requests and timings, and calling `raise_for_status` automatically for every request of a client.

**Transport adapters.** `Session.mount(prefix, adapter)` sends every URL that starts with `prefix` to that adapter, choosing the **longest matching prefix**. So `s.mount("https://api.example.com/", special)` replaces the default `https://` adapter for that one API only. An adapter subclasses `requests.adapters.BaseAdapter` (or `HTTPAdapter`), and implements `send(request, **kwargs)`, which returns a `Response`, plus `close()`.

Custom adapters power:

- per-host settings (different retries or pool sizes),
- caching (`requests-cache` and `CacheControl` work this way),
- transports without the network: serving `file://` URLs, passing requests straight to a Python web app inside the same program in tests, or talking to a local service through a Unix socket file (`requests-unixsocket`),
- simulating failures in tests.

When subclassing `HTTPAdapter`, override `send` and call `super().send(...)` so the normal behaviour still happens around your additions. Keep hooks fast and free of surprises: they run inside every request, so the caller waits for them.
concepts.code:
import requests
from requests.adapters import BaseAdapter

class StaticAdapter(BaseAdapter):
    """Answers every request locally; useful for tests or offline mode."""
    def send(self, request, **kwargs):
        resp = requests.Response()
        resp.status_code = 200
        resp._content = f'{{"echo": "{request.method} {request.path_url}"}}'.encode()
        resp.headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
        resp.url, resp.request = request.url, request
        return resp
    def close(self):
        pass

log = []
with requests.Session() as s:
    s.mount("https://api.example.com/", StaticAdapter())   # longest prefix wins
    s.hooks["response"].append(lambda r, *a, **kw: log.append(r.status_code))
    r = s.get("https://api.example.com/users?id=1", timeout=5)
    print(r.json())     # {'echo': 'GET /users?id=1'}
print(log)              # [200]
takeaways: The 'response' hook runs on every response and may replace it
mount(prefix, adapter) routes URLs by longest matching prefix
Custom adapters enable caching, test doubles and non-HTTP transports
pitfalls: Doing slow work (like calling another server) inside a response hook, which delays every request.

quiz.q: A session has adapters mounted at 'https://' and 'https://api.example.com/'. Which handles https://api.example.com/v1/items?
quiz.explain: Requests picks the adapter with the longest matching prefix.
